subject: sampling poorly-constrained shape parameter for gamma distribution

messages.author: 8d1674b7b16af1b1
messages.subject: sampling poorly-constrained shape parameter for gamma distribution
parts:
I'm working with the variance-gamma (VG) process, which is a Lévy process where the increments between t and t+1 are conditionally Gaussian with gamma-distributed variance (as opposed to Student t's _inverse_ gamma).  I'm getting really bad behavior from the gamma distribution's shape parameter, and I was wondering about possible reparameterizations of the gamma distribution. 

Basically, I think my problem boils down to this:

1. The shape parameter isn't well constrained by my data. Let's say it could be anywhere between 0.5 and 5 or so.

2. After transforming to the unconstrained scale, the gamma distribution's variance depends heavily on the shape parameter.

According to Wikipedia, Var[ln(X)] follows trigamma(shape). Plugging in my numbers from above, that means the variance could be anywhere between about 5 and 1/5. So we're getting toward Funnel territory in terms of the geometry, I think.

I also get strong correlations between the shape parameter and energy__ (along with BFMI warnings), which could indicate that there's an additional problem.

I've included a tiny reproducible example that just focuses on the shape parameter and sidesteps all the VG-specific stuff. I've also attached an rstan pairs() plot. It doesn't show the same shape/energy correlation I just mentioned, so it might not include all of the pathologies of the full model, but it's certainly simple.

Is there a way to reparameterize the gamma distribution to avoid this behavior? Otherwise, I think I might have to choose between a very strong prior, sampling from the VG distribution directly with Metropolis-Hastings, or something else unpalatable.

Thanks in advance!

Dave


parameters {
  real<lower=0> shape;
  real<lower=0> y;
}
model {
  shape ~ lognormal(0, 1);
  y ~ gamma(shape, shape);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling poorly-constrained shape parameter for gamma distribution
parts:
With a low step size (0.01) and high adapt delta (0.99), I don't
get any divergent transitions and everything seems to work in your simple
example. I added an MC simulation for comparison:

generated quantities {
real shape2 = lognormal_rng(0, 1);
real y2 = gamma_rng(shape2, shape2);
}


and get this with 4 chains of 10K iterations total (half warmup each):

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
shape 1.64 0.03 2.00 0.14 0.52 1.01 1.96 7.11 3357 1
y 1.00 0.01 1.34 0.00 0.25 0.70 1.30 3.92 8246 1
shape2 1.66 0.02 2.25 0.14 0.51 1.00 1.96 7.21 20000 1
y2 0.99 0.01 1.30 0.00 0.24 0.69 1.28 3.94 20000 1

You can see that the intervals are very close even if the sd is
a bit off (sampling error, not a bug).

The pairs plot does look like a pretty awful L shape on the constrained
scale --- I'm not good enough at R to figure out how to do the pairs() plot
on the unconstrained scale, which is the only scale that matters for
sampling.

Maybe someone else will have a better idea of how to reparameterize.
It's not a simple location-scale family, so the obvious non-centered
approach won't work. I also have no idea if you can integrate out that
shape parameter.

- Bob

unconstrained scale. You get a very extreme funnel shape
that's slightly asymmetric, so it's going to be a problem in
general without a reparameterization.

messages.author: 8d1674b7b16af1b1
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling poorly-constrained shape parameter for gamma distribution
parts:
Thanks Bob! Good to get confirmation that this is a funnel issue and I'm 
not missing something obvious. Also thanks for pointing out that I can get
some improvement by playing with the control parameters.

I can't think of a way that the shape parameter could be integrated out, 
so reparameterization might be the only good option. I feel like this
must have come up for someone before, and someone smart would
have figured it out, but my searches come up empty.

Thanks again,

Dave
